title: Breaches of the Accounts Rules and the duty to correct
subtitle: Recognising the recurring breach patterns, and why prompt replacement mitigates but never cures
objectives: Recognise the recurring breach patterns: transferring costs before delivering a bill, an individual client ledger going overdrawn, a mixed receipt paid entirely into the business account, and client money left outside the client account without authority
State the r 6 duty to correct a breach promptly on discovery, and explain what correction actually requires

Apply the distinction between mitigation and cure to a fact pattern, and explain why prompt replacement of missing funds reduces the seriousness of a breach without ever making the breach not have happened

leadingAuthorities.role: Imposes the duty to correct a breach promptly on discovery, including replacing any shortfall on the client account

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can define what a breach is once it is pointed out to them on the page. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You can spot a breach once it's labelled — this lesson is about spotting it inside a routine-looking fact pattern before anyone tells you.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the underlying r 6 rule here before. The test pool below leans on fact patterns that look like ordinary bookkeeping until you check the sequence — expect to spot the breach yourself.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 2 and hold the four recurring patterns in mind as a checklist before moving on — the rest of the lesson assumes you can name all four without prompting.

overview.hook: A cashier notices, three weeks after the event, that a client ledger went £40 overdrawn for two days before a receipt cleared. The shortfall is topped up from the business account within the hour of being spotted. Has anything actually gone wrong here — and if so, does fixing it that fast make it not have happened?
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The r 6 duty to correct, and the recurring breach patterns covered in this lesson, are settled and stable features of the current Accounts Rules; this lesson does not flag any contested point of law, though firms' internal escalation and reporting thresholds for what counts as 'material' vary and are a matter of firm policy rather than the rules themselves.

parts.heading: Why the same four breaches keep recurring
parts.voice: structural — sets the frame before naming the patterns
body: The SRA Accounts Rules 2019 have only 13 rules, and the great majority of reported breaches fall into a small handful of recurring patterns rather than exotic new scenarios. That's useful for an exam, and for practice: if you can recognise the shape of these patterns quickly, most breach questions stop being about memorising rule numbers and start being about spotting a familiar sequence hidden inside routine-sounding facts.

The four patterns this lesson works through are: transferring costs from the client account before a bill has actually been delivered; an individual client's ledger going overdrawn, even briefly; a mixed receipt (part client money, part the firm's own money) paid entirely into the business account instead of being split; and client money left outside the client account without proper authority to hold it there.

Each pattern breaches a different specific rule, but they share a common feature worth noticing early: none of them requires dishonesty. Every one of these can happen, and regularly does happen, through an ordinary administrative slip — a bill sent a day late relative to a transfer, a receipt processed before a bank account is checked, a payment logged to the wrong ledger. Recognising a breach is not the same as alleging misconduct, and the duty to correct exists precisely because breaches of this kind are routine.

components.definition: Any failure to comply with the SRA Accounts Rules, whether or not it involves dishonesty or causes actual client loss — an administrative slip that is corrected within minutes is still, technically, a breach, though a minor and swiftly remedied one.

interaction.prompt: Does a breach of the SRA Accounts Rules require dishonesty on the part of the person responsible?
options: No — most reported breaches are administrative slips with no dishonesty involved
Yes — the rules only apply where money has been dishonestly taken
Yes, but only for breaches involving the business account
interaction.trapExplanation: It's tempting to assume 'breach' implies wrongdoing in the moral sense. It doesn't — an overdrawn ledger caused by a receipt clearing a day late is a breach the moment it happens, regardless of anyone's state of mind.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — dishonesty is a separate, much more serious question. Most breaches are ordinary administrative failures.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — a breach is defined by the failure to comply with the rule, not by anyone's intentions. Keep that distinction in mind as you work through the patterns below.

parts.heading: Pattern one and two: transferring before the bill, and the overdrawn ledger
parts.voice: worked-example — walks each pattern through with figures
body: Transferring before the bill: a firm may only transfer money from the client account to the business account in respect of costs once it has actually delivered a bill (or other written notification of the costs) to the client. A firm that completes work worth £2,000, transfers £2,000 out of the client account the same afternoon, and emails the bill the following morning has breached this sequencing requirement — the transfer happened before the client had any documented notice of what was being charged, even though the amount transferred turned out to be exactly right.

The overdrawn individual ledger: client money belonging to different clients must never be used to cover a shortfall on another client's ledger, and no individual client ledger should show a debit balance — money going out that the ledger doesn't show as having come in yet. A firm that pays out £5,000 on a client's matter on the (correct) assumption that a £5,000 receipt is 'definitely coming', only for the receipt to clear two days later, has let that client's ledger run overdrawn for two days — during which time, as a matter of bookkeeping reality, the shortfall was necessarily covered by other clients' money sitting in the same pooled client account.

Notice what both patterns have in common: the firm did nothing that harmed the client financially in either case — the transfer amount was correct, and the receipt did arrive. The breach lies in the sequencing, not the arithmetic. That is exactly why these patterns are easy to miss under exam pressure: the numbers on the page look fine.

components.label: Pattern check: transferring before the bill vs the overdrawn ledger
points: Transferring before the bill: the transfer date must come after (or coincide with) the date a bill or written notification is actually given to the client, not before
Overdrawn ledger: an individual client's ledger must never show money paid out exceeding money shown as received for that client, even briefly and even if a matching receipt is virtually certain
Both patterns can occur with the correct final numbers — the breach is about sequence and timing, not about whether the figures eventually balance
Both are typically discovered on a routine ledger reconciliation, not because a client complains

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that shows a breach has occurred, even though the final figures are correct.
interaction.scenarioText: A firm completes £1,500 of work for a client on Monday, transfers £1,500 from the client account to the business account on Monday afternoon, and sends the client a bill for exactly £1,500 on Tuesday morning.
tappableSpans: transfers £1,500 from the client account to the business account on Monday afternoon
sends the client a bill for exactly £1,500 on Tuesday morning
interaction.correctSpan: transfers £1,500 from the client account to the business account on Monday afternoon
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the breach — the transfer happened before the bill was delivered on Tuesday, regardless of the amount being exactly right.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at the order of events — the amount being correct doesn't matter here; what matters is whether the transfer came before or after the bill was actually delivered.

parts.heading: Pattern three and four: the mixed receipt, and money left outside the client account
parts.voice: technical — works through the split with figures
body: The mixed receipt: where a single payment received by a firm is part client money and part the firm's own money (for example, a cheque for £1,200 covering £800 of disbursements still to be paid on the client's behalf and £400 of the firm's own costs already billed), the whole £1,200 must be paid into the client account, and the firm's £400 share then transferred out promptly — or the payment must be split at the point of banking. What must not happen is banking the whole £1,200 straight into the business account on the reasoning that 'most of it is ours anyway once you net it off' — that leaves £800 of client money sitting in the wrong account entirely.

Client money left outside the client account without authority: client money must be paid into the client account promptly on receipt, without exception, unless a specific rule permits an alternative (for example, where the client has given informed, specific written agreement for the firm to hold funds elsewhere, such as in an account in the client's own name that the firm controls). A firm that receives a client's cheque for £10,000 and leaves it, uncashed and unbanked, in a physical file for a week while other work takes priority has breached this rule for every day the money sits there — even though nothing was ever at risk of being lost.

Both patterns often surface together in practice: a mixed receipt mishandled at the point of banking frequently results in client money then sitting in the business account for days or weeks before anyone notices, compounding a single moment of misclassification into an ongoing breach that continues for as long as it goes uncorrected.

components.text: Client money must be paid into a client account promptly on receipt, without exception, save where a specific provision of the rules permits an alternative arrangement. A receipt that is part client money and part the firm's own money must be paid into the client account as a whole, or split at the point of receipt, so that no part of the client's share is paid into the business account.
elements: Client money paid into the client account promptly on receipt
A mixed receipt is banked as client money unless split at the point of receipt
No part of a client's share of a mixed receipt reaches the business account
Exceptions require a specific rule and, where relevant, informed client agreement

interaction.prompt: A firm receives a single cheque for £2,400: £1,600 to cover a disbursement not yet paid, and £800 for the firm's own costs already billed and confirmed in a delivered bill. What is the compliant way to bank this?
options: Pay the whole £2,400 into the business account, since £800 of it is the firm's own money in any event
Pay the whole £2,400 into the client account, then promptly transfer out the £800 the firm is entitled to
Split the cheque before banking so that £800 never touches either account until the disbursement is paid
Pay £1,600 into the business account and £800 into the client account, reversing the correct allocation
interaction.explanation: The compliant route (absent splitting the cheque itself, which usually isn't physically possible with a single instrument) is to bank the whole receipt into the client account, then transfer out the firm's own £800 share promptly — never to bank client money into the business account on a netting-off basis.

parts.heading: The r 6 duty to correct: what 'promptly' actually requires
parts.voice: direct — sets up the standard the tests will probe
body: SRA Accounts Rules 2019, r 6 requires a firm to correct a breach promptly upon discovery. 'Promptly' is doing real work in that sentence: it is not 'eventually', 'at the next scheduled reconciliation', or 'when convenient' — it means as soon as the breach is identified, the firm must act, starting with replacing any shortfall in client money from the firm's own resources.

Correction has two elements that are easy to blur together: replacing any missing money (so that the client account, and each individual client ledger within it, is restored to the position it should have been in), and addressing the cause, so the same failure doesn't simply recur next week. A firm that tops up an overdrawn ledger but changes nothing about the process that let it go overdrawn has only done half the job.

The duty falls on whoever discovers the breach, most often the compliance officer for finance and administration (COFA), but the obligation to act promptly is not limited to a specific role — any partner or manager who becomes aware of a breach and does nothing is, at that point, compounding the original breach with a fresh failure to correct it.

components.title: What r 6 correction requires
components.description: The two elements of a compliant correction, once a breach is discovered.

nodes.label: Breach discovered (on reconciliation, audit, or otherwise)
Replace any shortfall promptly, from the firm's own resources if necessary
Identify and address the underlying cause
Both steps together = a compliant correction under r 6

components.textAlternative: Once a breach is discovered, r 6 requires two things done together: promptly replacing any shortfall in client money, from the firm's own resources if necessary, and identifying and addressing the underlying cause so the same failure does not recur. Doing only one of these is an incomplete correction.

interaction.prompt: A COFA discovers, during a routine reconciliation, that a client ledger has been £300 overdrawn for six days because a receipt was logged to the wrong client's ledger by mistake. The COFA immediately transfers £300 from the business account to correct the ledger, but does not investigate how the misallocation happened. Analyse whether the firm has complied with r 6.
factsToOrder: The ledger was £300 overdrawn for six days
The cause was a receipt logged to the wrong client's ledger
The COFA discovers this on routine reconciliation
The COFA does not investigate the underlying misallocation

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the firm has fully complied with its r 6 duty to correct the breach represented by the overdrawn ledger.
modelAnswer.rule: R 6 requires prompt correction on discovery, which has two elements: replacing any shortfall promptly, and identifying and addressing the underlying cause so the failure does not recur.
modelAnswer.application: Replacing the £300 promptly on discovery satisfies the first element well. But the COFA has not investigated how the receipt came to be misallocated — without that step, the same misallocation could recur on another client's ledger, and the underlying process failure remains unaddressed.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The firm has partially, but not fully, complied with r 6: the shortfall has been replaced promptly, but correction is incomplete until the underlying cause is identified and addressed.

parts.heading: Prompt replacement mitigates — it does not cure
parts.voice: argumentative — confronts the common misconception directly
body: Here is the point most students get wrong, and it is worth stating as bluntly as possible: replacing a shortfall promptly, however fast, does not make the breach not have happened. It is a mitigating step — relevant to how seriously the breach is viewed, and often decisive in whether the SRA treats it as an isolated slip rather than a pattern of concern — but it is not a cure, because the breach is defined by the rule having been broken, not by whether the money was eventually put right.

This distinction matters practically. A firm that discovers an overdrawn ledger and replaces the shortfall within the hour has behaved exactly as r 6 requires — and should be recognised as having done the right thing. But 'did the right thing after the breach' and 'there was no breach' are two different statements, and conflating them is the single most common error in how students describe these scenarios: writing an answer that concludes 'no breach occurred because it was fixed immediately' gets the analysis backwards.

The honest, complete answer has two parts, always: identify that a breach occurred (naming which rule and why), and separately assess the response — was it corrected promptly, was the shortfall replaced, was the cause addressed. A fast, complete correction is genuinely good practice and genuinely relevant to seriousness. It just isn't the same question as whether a breach happened at all.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often conclude 'no breach occurred' or 'the breach was cured' where a firm replaced a shortfall quickly, especially within the same day.
components.whyItsWrong: Speed of correction is a mitigating factor going to seriousness and to whether the SRA is likely to treat the matter as isolated — it is never a basis for concluding that no breach occurred. The breach is fixed in time at the moment the rule was broken; nothing that happens afterwards changes that fact, however fast or complete the fix.

interaction.prompt: In which scenario would it be correct to say 'a breach occurred, but it was promptly and fully corrected' rather than 'no breach occurred'?
interaction.scenarioA: A firm's ledger shows a client's money paid out only after the matching receipt had cleared into the client account that same morning, with no gap at any point.
interaction.scenarioB: A firm's ledger goes £900 overdrawn for four hours before a receipt clears; on discovering this at end-of-day reconciliation, the firm immediately replaces the shortfall and reviews why the payment was released early.
interaction.explanation: In B, the ledger did go overdrawn — a breach occurred the moment it happened — and the firm's fast, complete response (replacing the shortfall and reviewing the cause) is a textbook correction, not proof that nothing went wrong. In A, there was never a gap at all, so there is no breach to describe in the first place.

testPool.prompt: A firm replaces an overdrawn client ledger's shortfall within thirty minutes of discovering it. Does this mean no breach of the Accounts Rules occurred?
options: No — the breach occurred the moment the ledger went overdrawn; the fast replacement is a correction under r 6, not proof there was no breach
Yes — a breach corrected within the same day is treated as not having happened
Yes — replacement within one hour is deemed by the rules to prevent a breach arising
No, but only because the shortfall exceeded £100
testPool.explanation: The breach is fixed at the moment the rule was broken. Prompt, complete replacement under r 6 mitigates its seriousness but never means it did not occur.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best describes what the r 6 duty to correct requires on discovery of a breach involving a shortfall of client money?
options: Replacing the shortfall only, with no further action required
Replacing the shortfall promptly and identifying and addressing the underlying cause
Reporting the matter to the client before taking any internal action
Waiting until the next scheduled reconciliation before acting
testPool.explanation: R 6 correction has two elements done together: promptly replacing any shortfall, and addressing the cause so the same failure does not recur.

testPool.prompt: A firm transfers £1,800 in costs from the client account to the business account on the same day it completes the work, and sends the client a bill for exactly £1,800 the following day. Has a breach occurred?
options: No — since the amount transferred exactly matches the bill, there is nothing to correct
Yes — the transfer took place before the bill was delivered, breaching the sequencing requirement, regardless of the amount being correct
No — breaches of this kind only arise where the amount transferred is wrong
Yes, but only because the client was not told in advance that a transfer would happen
testPool.trapExplanation: The exactly-matching figure is designed to make this look like a non-issue. It isn't — the requirement is about timing (bill before transfer), not about whether the eventual numbers reconcile.
testPool.explanation: Transferring before delivering the bill breaches the sequencing rule even where, as here, the amount later billed is exactly correct.

testPool.prompt: A firm receives a cheque covering £500 of disbursements and £300 of its own billed costs, and pays the whole £800 into the business account, reasoning that 'the client authorised the disbursement payment anyway, so it comes out even.' Which best describes this?
options: Compliant — provided the client authorised the disbursement, banking the whole receipt into the business account is acceptable
A breach — the £500 client share should have gone into the client account, or the receipt split, regardless of the client's authorisation of the disbursement itself
Compliant, because the total figures 'come out even' once the disbursement is eventually paid
A breach, but only if the disbursement is not paid within 24 hours
testPool.trapExplanation: Client authorisation to pay a disbursement is a separate question from where the receipt itself must be banked. 'It evens out eventually' is exactly the netting-off reasoning that this pattern of breach turns on — the £500 was client money the moment it was received and had to be banked as such.
testPool.explanation: The £500 disbursement portion is client money that should have reached the client account; banking the whole mixed receipt into the business account on a netting-off basis is a breach regardless of any later authorisation to pay the disbursement.

testPool.prompt: A cashier notices a client ledger went £220 overdrawn for three days last month before a delayed receipt cleared, fully covering the shortfall. No client complained and the amount is now correct. Should this still be treated as a breach requiring correction under r 6?
options: No — since the receipt eventually cleared and no client complained, there is nothing to address
Yes — the ledger going overdrawn was itself a breach at the time, and the firm should still investigate why it happened even though the figures are now correct
No, because three days is within an acceptable grace period for receipts to clear
Yes, but only if the shortfall exceeds £500
testPool.explanation: The breach occurred the moment the ledger went overdrawn, regardless of whether a matching receipt later arrived and regardless of client complaint. R 6 still calls for the cause to be identified and addressed, even though no money is currently missing.

testPool.prompt: A client's cheque for £6,000 sits unbanked in a physical file for ten days because the fee earner forgot to pass it to the cashiers. On discovery, the cashier banks it immediately into the client account. What has occurred, and what has been done about it?
options: No breach occurred, since the money was never actually lost or at risk

A breach occurred for each day the money sat outside the client account; banking it immediately on discovery is a correct first step under r 6, though the cause (the internal handover failure) should also be addressed
A breach occurred only once, on day ten, when the cashier finally noticed
No breach occurred, provided the cheque itself was never lost or damaged
testPool.explanation: Client money must be paid in promptly on receipt; every day it sat unbanked was a continuing breach, not a single event on day ten. Banking it immediately on discovery is correct, but full r 6 compliance also means addressing why the handover failed.

testPool.prompt: A firm's COFA discovers a client ledger overdrawn by £150 and replaces the shortfall from the business account the same afternoon, but takes no further action because 'it's a small amount and it's fixed now.' Is this a complete r 6 correction?
options: Yes — the shortfall has been replaced, which is all r 6 requires
No — the shortfall was replaced, but the underlying cause has not been identified or addressed, so the correction is incomplete regardless of how small the amount was
Yes, because amounts under £200 are exempt from the requirement to investigate cause
No, because the COFA should have reported the matter to the client before replacing the shortfall
testPool.explanation: R 6 correction has two elements, and neither the size of the shortfall nor the speed of replacement removes the second: identifying and addressing the underlying cause. Skipping that step leaves the correction incomplete.

testPool.prompt: Under SRA Accounts Rules 2019, r 6, what is the significance of the word 'promptly' in the duty to correct a breach?
options: It sets a fixed 48-hour deadline for every correction
It requires action as soon as the breach is identified, not at the next scheduled reconciliation or when convenient
It only applies to breaches discovered by the COFA personally
It means the firm has discretion to decide when correction is convenient, provided clients are not told
testPool.explanation: 'Promptly' means acting as soon as the breach is identified — there is no fixed statutory number of hours or days, but 'eventually' or 'at the next scheduled reconciliation' falls short of the standard.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best describes the legal effect of a firm promptly and fully correcting a breach under r 6?
options: It retroactively means the breach never happened
It is a mitigating factor relevant to how seriously the breach is viewed, but the breach itself remains a fact that occurred
It transfers responsibility for the breach to whichever individual discovered it
It removes any obligation to record the breach internally
testPool.explanation: Correction mitigates seriousness — it can be the difference between an isolated slip and a pattern of concern — but it does not erase the fact that a breach occurred, and firms are still expected to keep an internal record of breaches and how they were addressed.

testPool.prompt: A partner becomes aware that a client ledger has been overdrawn for a week but takes no action, assuming someone else in finance will notice at the next reconciliation. How should this be characterised under r 6?
options: As entirely the finance team's responsibility, since the partner did not cause the original overdraft
As a fresh failure by the partner to correct promptly, in addition to the original breach that caused the overdraft
As acceptable, provided the reconciliation happens within the same month
As irrelevant, since only the COFA can be responsible for correction under r 6
testPool.explanation: The duty to correct promptly on discovery is not limited to whoever caused the original breach or holds a specific role — a partner who becomes aware and does nothing compounds the original breach with a separate failure to act.

testPool.prompt: A firm's bookkeeper spots that a £7,500 receipt was banked into the business account instead of the client account two days ago, because it was misclassified as the firm's own costs. She corrects the classification and moves the full £7,500 to the client account the same day. Has the firm fully discharged its r 6 duty?
options: Yes — moving the money to the correct account is all that r 6 requires
Not necessarily — the money has been correctly relocated, but the firm should also establish why the receipt was misclassified in the first place, to prevent recurrence
No — the firm must also report the matter to the client before the correction is valid
Yes, provided the correction happens within 24 hours of the original misclassification
testPool.trapExplanation: Moving the money looks like the whole job, and for many students that's where the analysis stops. But r 6 correction is two steps, not one — relocating the £7,500 addresses the shortfall, not the process failure that put it in the wrong account to begin with.
testPool.explanation: Relocating the money is the first, necessary step; a complete correction under r 6 also requires identifying and addressing why the misclassification happened.

testPool.prompt: A firm's ledger shows a payment of £3,000 made out to a third party on a client's matter one day before the matching £3,000 client receipt is shown as banked, though both transactions relate to the same afternoon and the receipt was, in fact, already sitting in the firm's bank account (just not yet posted to the ledger). Is this a breach?
options: No — since the money was already in the firm's bank account, there is no real shortfall regardless of the ledger's posting order
Yes — an individual client ledger must not show a payment out exceeding money shown as received for that client, and posting delay does not change that the ledger itself displayed an overdraw
No, because same-day transactions are always treated as simultaneous for r 6 purposes
Yes, but only if the receipt is never posted at all
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to reason from the underlying bank balance rather than the ledger itself — but the overdrawn-ledger pattern is assessed by reference to what the client's own ledger shows at any given time, not by netting off against the firm's overall bank position.
testPool.explanation: The client ledger itself showed a payment out before a matching receipt was posted, which is the overdrawn-ledger breach pattern, regardless of the underlying bank account having sufficient funds overall.

testPool.prompt: A trainee is asked to describe, in a file note, what happened when a client ledger went briefly overdrawn and was corrected the same day. Which is the most accurate way to phrase it?
options: 'No breach occurred because the shortfall was corrected the same day.'
'A breach occurred when the ledger went overdrawn; it was corrected the same day by replacing the shortfall and reviewing the cause.'
'The client ledger was always compliant, since the final balance is correct.'
'A breach may have occurred, but this cannot be confirmed without a formal SRA investigation.'
testPool.explanation: The accurate description names the breach as having occurred at the point the ledger went overdrawn, and separately records the correction — conflating the two into 'no breach occurred' is the most common analytical error in this area.

testPool.prompt: Which of these four is NOT one of the recurring breach patterns covered in this lesson?
options: Transferring costs from the client account before delivering a bill
An individual client ledger going overdrawn
A firm charging a client more in fees than was quoted at the outset of the matter
Client money left outside the client account without proper authority
testPool.explanation: Overcharging relative to a quote is a client care and costs information issue, not one of the four Accounts Rules breach patterns covered here — those are billing/transfer sequencing, overdrawn ledgers, mixed receipts, and money left outside the client account.

testPool.prompt: A firm argues that because none of its recent breaches involved any actual loss to a client, none of them needed to be corrected under r 6. Is this consistent with the rules?
options: Yes — r 6 only applies where a client has suffered an identifiable financial loss
No — the r 6 duty to correct arises from the breach itself, not from whether it happened to cause a client any identifiable loss
Yes, provided the firm's insurer confirms no claim is likely
No, but only for breaches involving more than one client's ledger at once
testPool.explanation: The duty to correct is triggered by the breach, not by proof of loss — many of the recurring patterns in this lesson (transferring before a bill, a brief overdraw later covered) involve no actual loss to the client at all, and still require correction.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is concluding 'no breach occurred' wherever a firm corrected a shortfall quickly. Say what actually happened instead: a breach occurred at a specific point, and it was then corrected — mitigation and non-occurrence are never the same finding.
